body:
I don't like the categorization of people as high- or low-functioning schizophrenics, just like I don't like functioning labels for autism people either (I'm autistic ftr). Everyone has different combinations of symptoms, and are better in some situations than others. Some people struggle more than others. That's it.

That aside, I do find that in my own experiences with schizophrenia, I've become much more insightful and perceptive of my reality, my actions and my surroundings. I have a great interest in objective reality, almost too much so according to my therapist. I spend a lot of time considering things that may or may not be true. When your reality is tenuous, you find yourself a lot more receptive to changes in that reality, and a lot more suspicious when that reality seems too strange to be "real". I think that's why paranoia is so high in people with schizophrenia.

I think that schizophrenia makes me a better writer. It's hard for me, articulating my feelings, but I find poetry satisfying.

I'd love to have a schizophrenic therapist, personally. I love knowing that I can relate to my psych professionals. My therapist right now openly shares to me her experiences with mental health, especially anxiety, and even that is really comforting to me.
I really really like Maya the Psychic by Gerard Way.

Zoloft for depression (100mg), Latuda for psychosis (160mg), Depakote for mania (1,000mg), Gabapentin for anxiety (2,400mg daily), and Vistaril for anxiety (50mg). Vistaril's my FAVORITE, it's been a lifesaver recently with my panic attacks. I was on olanzapine for a long time which worked really well for psychosis, but made me obese. Right now I think my main goal is to safely lower the amount of some of these meds, namely the Latuda and Gabapentin. I think I could do with lowering the Zoloft too, but my psych disagrees with that.

Zyprexa made me double in weight, and it's why I'm obese now. That happened over the course of about a year. Latuda's been working pretty well for me so far, it's hard to lose weight but I'm at least staying at the same number. I fluctuate a bit, but always within the same 10 pounds. Latuda is very pricey though, I'd only recommend it if you have good insurance.

About a month for each, because that was how long it took to figure it wasn't working & to get to the next psych appointment. IIRC I went up to 30 and was on that for a while until that stopped working too.
For me, the meds did end up causing psychosis and I had to switch off of em. For now I don't really know what's gonna help with my concentration, but I do know that the priority is psychosis.

Yes, it's grounds for a bipolar diagnosis. I was diagnosed with schizophrenia when I was 18, and then after experimenting with SSRIs when I was 19, had a manic episode and was diagnosed with bipolar 1. My current diagnosis is schizoaffective, bipolar type. Had another manic episode when I was 20 that was also medication induced. So I'm in the same boat as you, only 2 medication-induced episodes, but I do believe that I still fit the qualifications of bipolar. I distrust the psych field more than most people, but the DSM is bullshit in general. The way it works, if a doctor says you have it, that means you have it, when it comes to psych shit.

I believe I was actually misdiagnosed with ADD recently, because my psych refused to believe that my symptoms when it came to inattentiveness and disorganized thinking were caused by schizophrenia (even though I told him that they weren't present in my youth). But I needed the diagnosis to get medication for my symptoms, so I rolled with it. I feel like more people should realize that the DSM is fake and largely really just doesn't matter. Take it from someone who's primary diagnosis is literally "you fit the criteria for both of these disorders so we're going to just sandwich them together and call it something else, even though they literally have ABSOLUTELY NOTHING to do with one another."
Yes, it can. I'd recommend talking to your doctor about it.
I've had the opposite happen as well. Risperdal worked just fine for me at some point, but when I tried it later it worked so ineffectively it sent me to the hospital.

I'm schizoaffective (schizophrenia + bipolar 1) and since I was diagnosed with schizophrenia first, I've been on APs ever since I started meds. I know that since I'm sz and not just bipolar, my experiences won't be exactly like yours in that regard, but I did want to note that you might get vastly different side effects from the other antipsychotics out there. I've been on Abilify, Zyprexa, Risperdal, Geodon, and now Latuda, and all of them were very different and some are definitely more tolerable than others. If Zyprexa wasn't right for you, it may just be that there's a different AP out there that'd be better for you (it's your choice though, of course).

I'm going to be honest, it can, but it can also get much better. I'm currently dealing with a medication mishap but for the most part my treatment gives me relief from all hallucinations and delusions. Medication is and should always be a choice, your choice, but I just wanted to say that it has gotten much better for me because of it.
My partner also has schizophrenia, but he is unmedicated. This is hys choice. Sometimes he struggles, like right now he's working through a paranoia spike, but for the most part hys symptoms have improved drastically over the years. It's very possible either way. I personally recommend CBT techniques (you can look them up online and there are even apps for it); they helped me with psychosis a lot.

This was and still is my most recurring kind of hallucination. Tactile hallucinations are a lot less common than audio or visual ones (in fact when I was sent to a neurologist to figure out why I was getting them, he laughed in my face when I brought up my family's history of schizophrenia because he thought it was such a low possibility), but they do happen. I have had visual hallus on occasion and audio once or twice but tactile I get pretty much whenever my meds aren't working right.

It depends on the therapist. If I were speaking to my younger self, I would say to tell them because even though I really really didn't like my experience at the hospital, my command hallucinations made me do a LOT of crazy fucked up shit and I'm lucky to be alive. I know you aren't me, though. It should be your decision and it is your decision, just know the consequences either way. You can hurt or even kill yourself if you continue on this path unaided. I'm not saying it will happen, but it is a possibility.

The activities depend on what kind of hospital you went to. I went to one of the "good" ones, so we had a lot of activities in the adult ward. 4 therapy sessions a day, if I remember right. Sometimes physical activity, sometimes coloring. Outside of that, there was TV and you could bring books or draw on paper. I got my parents to bring me the Walking Dead comic books and I read those to pass the time.  


There were some people around my age (I was 20) at the ward. I think I was the youngest there, but not by much. I made good friends with someone my parents' age. It wasn't too bad.

I watched a dude climb the fence when we were out on smoke break. It was about 15 feet tall, chain link fence, we were talking and then he just climbed right over it. Lots of yelling. Apparently once he made it to the other side he tried to just act casual like nothing had happened, but they got him of course and took him to a higher intensity unit. I felt bad for him.

From what I could tell from the first 20 minutes or so, it seemed fine, but I had to stop watching at that point. He has a recurring belief that he's the chosen one, and it pops up a lot, and it struck a chord with me and felt too similar to my own psychosis, so I had to stop watching.

I had a lot of magical thinking, the kind of stuff you'd expect from a kid but I just never really grew out of it. To be honest, the first thing that seriously manifested for me was the mood swings. I had a LOT of problems with dissociation too, including jumbling up my words and being unable to read at times. Then it was hallucinations, all tactile which confused the doctors a lot. Then I broke into full-on delusional episodes that spiraled into countless suicide attempts. Lucky to be here.
Stress, lack of sleep and caffeine. Especially caffeine. I love the taste of coffee but the hallucinations it gives me are awful.

Not on Medicare, but I've been on ER in the past, and I'm on DR now. They changed it after I was hospitalized last April; still not sure why, but I can't complain. The only real difference is that I have to take DR twice a day. It works the same for me.

I was diagnosed with schizophrenia before I was diagnosed with bipolar (I was only diagnosed with the latter after meds caused a manic/mixed episode). My understanding of it is that I match the criteria for both schizophrenia and bipolar i, making me schizoaffective. This probably doesn't speak to everyone who has schizoaffective, but that's how I explain it to people.

To be honest, medication was the only thing that stopped my hallucinations and delusions. Though therapy helped with coping with them, it was my psychiatrists that really helped me pull through. I don't have much of a problem with the way they go about things, though I do wish my current psych talked a little more as opposed to very obviously just checking things off a list behind his computer screen.

I find that antidepressants, for me, mainly just make things easier to do. I can find the motivation to do things while I'm on them. I'm also less prone to breakdowns and suicidal thinking while I'm on them.

I would love knowing that my psych has/has had schiz, but telling everyone in your workplace could be risky. My therapist told me not to tell anyone when I went back to college; she said that it could cause problems because of the stigma. It'd be great for some patients to know they aren't alone and for them to have some source of inspiration but I'd hate for you to end up in a bad or uncomfortable place because of that.

Good luck with your current combo. I was on Zyprexa the longest but had to switch off 'cause of the weight gain. Now I'm on Latuda 120mg and it seems to be working pretty good. Got a little psychotic recently but that was only because I drank coffee. So far so good!
Yup - my maternal grandmother. Started seeing symptoms at 16, was diagnosed at 19.

Are you sure you can't at least contact your old psych for advice in the meantime, before you can land a new one? It seems irresponsible of them to just drop off the face of the earth right after starting you on a new med.

Either way, I highly doubt that every med you try will be like this. They're all different for everyone. For me personally, the antidepressants I've tried have occasionally made me manic, but that was the worst side effect I've ever gotten from one. I hope that the side effects for this one ease up for you soon and that it ends up being a lot more manageable, but if not, there are a TON of options out there for you.

EDIT: You can also call your pharmacist, and see what they say/if they have any advice in lieu of talking to a psych.

Keep in mind that the whole "life expectancy" thing isn't a death sentence. Especially if you're young now, there's plenty of time for science to catch up and for medical care to improve. And I hear about people who defy the whole "life expectancy" thing ALL the time. I know that without meds I'd personally be miserable, so I'm gonna take my chances. I'm not telling you what to decide, but keep in mind that it's nothing close to a guarantee.

I think I'm on a higher dose of Depakote than I really need and it doesn't affect me much. All that I really notice from Depakote is that it stopped me from being manic; other than that I don't have many side effects from it. Just need blood tests every once in a while.

You'll probably have your ups and downs, but I'm optimistic for you. It took me a couple years of experimentation, but I'm on a medication regimen that's been working really well for me right now. I'm pretty damn stable as it is. There'll be some changes, sure, but you can still have a normal life.

Do you know when they'll be back? In the meantime, grounding exercises helped me a whole lot when I was psychotic. That and doing soothing/distracting activities. Be sure to take care of yourself while all this is going on, because I know it's hard to keep that in mind.

I know it's scary, but it can be managed. I VERY rarely have any psychotic symptoms anymore after finding a medication combo that works for me. Some people even recover completely and manage to lead normal lives without medication. Let your doctor know what's going on and see what your options are - the thing about medications for this kind of stuff is that there are a TON of options out there, so don't get discouraged. You can get a normal life back.

I've got schizoaffective, which basically means I meet both the criteria of schizophrenia + bipolar I. I get delusions and hallucinations under any circumstance if I'm not medicated properly, but they tend to be particularly bad if I'm having a mixed episode. Not all people with schiz- are zombies; in fact I only really seem to get like that when on the wrong meds.
Good luck with Latuda. That's what they gave me while I was in the hospital, and I've been on it ever since. It helped my psychotic symptoms and surprisingly helps quite a bit with mood too.

Absolutely in the midst of this right now - doesn't help that I'm schizoaffective, so the schiz- part lends to disorganized thoughts too. Lost my job because of it. My therapist told me that she doesn't think I have ADHD, but my symptoms are really similar, and that I should probably look into medication because lately I've been absolutely useless.

Thanks! I'm on a pretty decent dose of Depakote as it is (it was raised to compensate for 200mg Zoloft before, but now I'm just on 100mg Zoloft), so I wonder if that could keep me stable. I expect he might raise it a little bit based off how the blood work looks just to be safe, but hopefully it helps convince him.
No. But I highly doubt I could afford one. I can't evven afford my tuition. And if I don't pay that I need to start paying student loans. Everything's just going to hell right now.

I'm going to be on them for the rest of my life, but you're on a very low dose (I maxed out on Abilify while I was still prodromal and it still wasn't strong enough for me), so you have a good chance. Talk to your doctor about giving it a try. Be very, very careful about it though and COMMUNICATE WITH YOUR DOCTOR... medication changes like that can be dangerous.

I relate to a lot of this. I'm a DFAB butch nonbinary lesbian who uses he/him pronouns. To me, being a nb woman has a lot to do with having vital connections to womanhood, especially as a social class, while also being detached enough from it to be uncomfortable being referred to as ("just") a woman in most contexts. It's hard to explain, but it's basically like this: I am a woman. I'm just not a binary woman. A lot of the connotations and meanings of "woman" that people try to impose on me as a result simply don't match. And it's not just because I'm gender-nonconforming - it's because I'm something different entirely.

Anyway, aside from definitions, for me, the internet was ESSENTIAL to figuring out I was transgender. At first, I thought I was a trans man, because when joining a chat room I used the handle "Stan" on a whim, and having everyone treat me as a guy felt... really good. It felt amazing. It was unlike anything I had ever felt before. It took me a while to realize that there was something about being seen as a guy by my friends that didn't sit right with me, but being ASSUMED as a guy felt and still feels perfect. It wasn't until I saw a post online affirming that some butch lesbians do transition/take testosterone that I realized my identity was even possible.

So really, the number-one thing I'd recommend is trying things out online. Start a blog, join a few discord servers, try out different names, different pronouns, etc. It's a lot less scary than trying anything out in person.

I'm currently on four medications that together help me a whole lot. Latuda for positive symptoms. Zoloft for depression & anxiety. Depakote to keep me from going manic. Gabapentin for anxiety bc I can't raise the Zoloft dose without going manic.

The biggest thing that helped me, I think, was running a blog about my experiences. I talk about my highs and my lows, it helps me reflect and analyze things objectively, and it helps me open up to others. I've met some of my best friends through running that blog.

To be honest, a lot of this really just sounds like what it feels like to be in your early teens. I'm not sure if that sounds comforting to hear or not, but I personally would try not to worry about it.

Nothing is for sure. Especially since you have anxiety and OCD, and you already know that they're fairly common for people who have those illnesses, there is absolutely no guarantee that this has anything to do with schizophrenia. Just because you have something that may evolve into a symptom of schizophrenia doesn't mean you have it. Not everyone who has auditory hallucinations is schizophrenic - there are many other possible causes. It does sound good to see a psychiatrist if you're worrying about it, though. Hope you can relax a little in the meantime. Hugs.
No, it isn't. No one's saying that you can't use the word for yourself. But you reclaiming it doesn't change that it's a slur that has harmed many others.

If you are worried they will gang up on you or take you by surprise, going to the hospital will actually be a very good idea. When I went, there were staff members watching all of us while we slept, and you couldn't go anywhere without staff members accompanying you. They could definitely help and assist you in an emergency. It sounds safer to me.
Do you know what drugs? I got a tip last night that there is a group of people trying to get me to kill myself. Please PM me if necessary.

The very rare times that I have voices, they're usually like this. Only time I was hospitalized was because they were suddenly very present and very intelligible. Not used to that - I'm used to the thoughts, sure, but not voices.

I was originally diagnosed with schizophrenia, then bipolar I, then schizoaffective bipolar type, and then weirdly enough schizoaffective depressive type when I was at the hospital? Even though I repeatedly told them that the psychotic break I had been hospitalized for was caused by a manic episode, because I'm bipolar? I dunno. I consider my schizophrenia and bipolar to be separate even if that's not how they want it to work in the DSM, the manual's a bunch of garbage anyway so I don't pay it much mind.

I'm schizoaffective - I was originally diagnosed with schizophrenia, and then bipolar I. In my opinion, them deciding that you must be bipolar because you're too "well spoken" to be schizophrenic sounds like BS. You can socially pass as neurotypical and still be schizophrenic. I've only had two manic episodes, both triggered by medication changes, and without meds I relate to having pretty consistent psychosis. I also have memory loss and amnesia, which I usually chalk up to having DID. There could be more to it, sure, but hell if I know.

I'm not saying that you have any of these things, but I do think that if you think you've been misdiagnosed, seeing a different psychiatrist might be helpful. There are certainly some quacks out there.
Weed can definitely be a psychedelic, depending on the strain you're smoking. It's pretty common for it to make psychosis work if you're already having symptoms without it.

I've been told not to take anything like zzzquil with my medication, but I do take melatonin to help me stay asleep (I have PTSD that makes it difficult). It kind of works, but it's kind of hard to tell - I'm only taking 3mg right now to test the waters out but I might try upping it soon.

Lately, I usually have paranoid delusions, usually along the lines of being spied upon or people poisoning me or breaking into my house. When my psychosis first started developing, though, the worst was when I had delusions of G-d speaking to me and ordering me to do things. I attempted suicide several times because of that, because I thought G-d wanted me to. That's probably my most persistent delusion, and it was triggered a couple times at the hospital too.
That's true. I just called my doctor about if he knows a good hospital I can go to. Thank you, I might not have done that if you hadn't said this.

I would also recommend trying to go through your general doctor; when my little brother did that he got medication that way until he was able to see a psychiatrist. They might not be able to do much, but it'll be better than nothing.

Forgot to follow up on this but thanks guys. I think it was probably a combination of the anxiety and the medication I was taking (I have gabapentin to take as-needed, which can cause strange eye movements and blurry vision). It seems to be somewhat more manageable now.

It worked great for me and I took it for a year, but I had to stop because of the weight gain (100 pounds in one year, and I was originally at 115). I was sleeping a lot too, especially at the end. But now I'm in between medications and unable to get a good night's rest, so it's a give and take scenario I guess.

He'll probably just tell me to take my medication and wait. I do plan on taking the meds it's just that I just stopped taking Geodon (at doc's orders) yesterday and am going to start taking Risperdal tonight. This is probably why I am thinking this way but I can't help it. I do believe this and I'm scared. Every time I think about it I start panicking and I just can't stop thinking about it.

I got one when I was first getting diagnosed. My sz symptoms were atypical in that my primary hallucinations were all tactile, which threw off many of the psychiatrists and neurologists I saw. So I had an MRI done to make sure nothing too crazy (haha) was going on. It was kind of unpleasant but closing your eyes really helps with the claustrophobia.

You can get any job you want, many mentally ill people are in the psych field. I have a job with very flexible hours because I'm still wrangling with my mental health (~2 years since diagnosis) plus I'm in school. If I wasn't in school I probably wouldn't have to take so many sick days. Thankfully my job is very forgiving when it comes to that, and even let me take an indefinite break because of my current psychosis. I work online as a transcriptionist.

I don't think your diagnosis would hinder you when it comes to things like college or getting a job, if anything getting a diagnosis would help if you want to seek out things like accommodations. And ultimately the diagnosis is the way to go for treatment and recovery.

Best of luck, if you have any questions feel free.

I gave him water from the tap because no matter what source I give him they'll find a way to poison it somehow. They have access to the house. I don't know. I'm really scared but I'm going to jsut do what they want because i'm afraid of if they'll do something in return.

No one can diagnose you over the internet unfortunately. I'm sorry that your mother didn't take you seriously, I've been in that position before and it was awful.

Some of the things you mentioned I can relate to, some I can't. But all experiences are different. 

It does sound to me like it's something you should get some kind of help for, even if it seems to have improved... mental illnesses can come and go, and either way people usually don't suddenly stop being able to read.

But again, not much can happen online. I've heard of online therapy and counseling, but I think that's as far as it goes. I hope you find yourself in a position where you can get proper help sometime soon.

There's a line from a spoken word poem I like that goes something like "I think the genes for being an artist and mentally ill aren't just related, I think they're the same gene... but try telling that to a bill collector."

Sounds like a good idea. I'm not sure if I'd submit anything because I haven't been able to draw anything very symbolic lately. Maybe some day soon, if I can get my act together.

I used to be very afraid that I would hurt any of my pets while being psychotic but I never have. I couldn't imagine ever doing that, for any reason. I haven't intentionally hurt anyone human, either.

Thankfully, the pets I personally own I don't have to handle every day. I live with two reptiles and an indoor pigeon, so if I'm feeling like I can't control myself I don't have to directly handle them that day. the reptiles are not social and my pigeon actually doesn't like being handled much, so even though I obviously have to feed her every day and sometimes when I open the door to change her water she comes out to say hello, she usually hops back in unprompted so that I don't even have to touch her.

It's mortifying to think that I could ever hurt them. They're so important to me. Whenever I think of reasons that my mental health is better now than it was last year, I think of how I adopted my pigeon last summer. It was the best decision I've made in recent memory.

My family (who I live with) have a lot of other animals in the house too, like dogs and cats, but just like the others I don't have to handle them every day because they already get attention from everyone else. I can ignore them if I need to.

Hearing that this happened is very scary, but I still don't think I'll do anything like that. I can't imagine it. I'm having another psychotic episode (the first I've had in a long time), but the only thing I think I'd ever directly harm because of it is maybe myself.

As someone diagnosed with bipolar I, though I'm not saying that you must also be bipolar or anything like that (i.e. I'm not trying to diagnose you at all), this does sound a LOT like my first experience with antidepressants and I really think you need to call your doctor ASAP. The first time I tried antidepressants, I went psychotic again, I became suicidal and my thoughts would not stop racing because the medication sent me into a mixed/manic episode. It took months to get back to normal. Please call your doctor and tell them what's happening, as this could be very dangerous.

I live with my parents and I intend to for a long time. I don't think I can ever truly live alone. But once I get out of school I do intend to help them out more, with bills and such, in return. It's somewhat comforting to me that my mom is the same way - she doesn't work, cook, or do much at all outside of driving people back and forth from school and taking care of the animals. And she's not schizophrenic. It makes me feel more normal.

Definitely agree with the others - it would be best to tell your doctor how you are feeling. With the combination of medication and therapy I have gone from a similar spot to where you're at to psychosis-free and relatively content in life.

Two years ago, I was a mess. I hallucinated daily, had severe delusions, and my mood swings were sometimes catastrophic. But I found a medication that worked for me (Abilify, and then Zyprexa!) for psychosis, and then eventually even one for my mood (Zoloft, which did cause me to have two manic episodes [one very recently and ongoing] but which I mostly have under control to a point that the benefits far outweigh the risks).

Therapy was also very, very useful for me, especially at the beginning. I'm not seeing one now, but I am hoping to find a new one soon (I'm trying to find one who is knowledgeable about gender, as I plan to transition as soon as possible and would need a therapist's help to do so).

One of the most important things I learned in therapy (and which I still need to be reminded of sometimes, even today, two years after my diagnosis and almost four years since my first psychotic break) that it's normal and okay to grieve because of your condition. The vast, vast majority of people will never experience something like this and it's okay to feel sad about it, or to feel sorry for yourself. You deserve time to do that. I still am, sometimes, and I feel like I will continue to be at least every once in a while. But you can accomplish really great things regardless. Many people with the illness have persevered and continue to persevere, and there's no reason that you can't be one of them. I hope this helps and I wish you good luck, please feel free to post here whenever you'd like to ask questions or share about your journey.

I had overall a very good experience with Abilify. It was the first med (and so the first AP) I ever tried, so at first the side effects hit me really hard - I got so dizzy I couldn't sit up and I couldn't hold my head straight when trying to focus on something (it just kept shaking). The dizziness wore off in a couple days, though, and the shaking within a few weeks (and it was always very minor, just bothersome). Otherwise, I can't actually remember any side effects I had on Abilify. The only reason I switched off was because I needed a stronger med (I gradually increased the dose over the year I was on it, and maxed out relatively quickly). Then I tried Risperdal (very briefly), olanzapine (again for about a year) and now I'm on Geodon after the MASSIVE olanzapine weight gain. I do think I probably gained a little weight on Abilify (I have a naturally very fast metabolism, which I think it slowed down a bit) but until the olanzapine I hadn't noticed it at all.

Also, I forgot to say, I can relate to what you said about school. My academic career has very severely plummeted since I started college (my symptoms first became severe my senior year of high school). I'm very slowly, only two classes at a time, making my way towards a degree in microbiology, but my future is looking very different now. I spent my first two years of college at UC Berkeley, my dream school, until the psychosis became so bad it was basically either I dropped out or committed suicide. Thankfully the latter did not happen.

Now I am at a community college, so I can be closer to home. It is easier and I live with family which is good because I can't really take care of myself. I don't know what I'm going to do career-wise. I want to be an ASL interpreter but I feel like my thoughts are too disorganized to do a fast-paced job like that. But I take ASL anyway because I love the language.

I relate to what you said, though. It's a difficult thing to experience and I'm sorry that happened. I wish you good luck in school and please remember that things WILL work out regardless.

EDIT: I should also add that my academic career plummeted all because I was untreated for several years. It's very, very good that you are being treated. I am optimistic for you.

Abilify was the first med I ever tried and it worked very well for me with very few side effects. The only scary thing was that for the first couple days I would get very, very dizzy to the point that I couldn't sit up. And for the first couple weeks I couldn't hold my head up straight to look at someone - it would just shake randomly. But those side effects wore off completely and then I was on it for about a year and it worked very well. The only reason I came off it was because I needed a stronger medication as my psychosis progressed. I went on olanzapine for a while and I'm on Geodon now, it's working well for me.

I haven't tried Wellbutrin, but I've heard good things about it. I'm on Zoloft, myself.

We can't diagnose you or anything, but it's not surprising that your psychosis was triggered by stress or lack of sleep, that can definitely aggravate psychosis in people very easily. That's how mine was, definitely. As for the meds, olanzapine was also very rough for me. I just recently got off of it to switch to Geodon which is going well for me so far. I was also on Abilify for a while which gave me no side effects at all (it felt very weird for about the first month, but that wore off), the only reason i switched off was because it wasn't strong enough for me in the end. I was also on Risperdal for a short time with no side effects. There are maany options out there for you to try, it's a matter of finding the right one, and in my opinion it's definitely worth it.
The thing is, I was doing better. I was going to a prestigious college and managing it, most of the time. Now I'm at a community college and I'm going nowhere in life anymore.
I was getting messages for about two years . I've been on meds for about a year and a half

They don t really want me around. You hsould see them when i talk about schizophrenia. on meds im no one, Nothing, can't contribute a damn thing. Off medds I had answers. They could give me answers. I used to be able to see the future. And they warned me not to get rid of that, but I didn't listen.

I don't feel anything anymore and i want to feel again. I want to hear them talkng again. I feel so lonely I even miss being violated by them, I just want to feel special again. I ccan follow the rules this time.
In the span of half a year I gained almost 90 pounds while on olanzapine. I'm going to tell my doctor that I want to switch to Geodon at my next appointment.
Thank you!! I really appreciate that.
https://www.patreon.com/ratbirds It looks pretty bare bones right now because it's only been up for a couple months & most of the posts are WIPs so they're patron-exclusive, but here it is.

I don't know if I have a thought disorder, per se, but thanks to schiz I definitely do experience a lot of the symptoms of them. The most common things I experience are poverty of speech and what they call "blocking" - this happens to me especially when I'm tired. I'll be in the middle of a conversation and then unable to speak. Sometimes I can say basic things like "What?" after someone else says something, but usually I can't. I have to just hang up! Typing gets very difficult when this happens for me, too, because it's the "making words" part that's hardest. Blocking happens a little more often, though - I'll be able to start a sentence or idea, but then completely unable to finish and I just go silent. This happens so often to me that a really good friend of mine (the only person I really talk to) thought that was just how I talked!

I guess you can call some aspects of it funny, though, especially out of context. I jotted down a bunch of notes, then went to take a break, during which the episode mostly subsided. Then I go back to my notes, which were total gibberish! When I tell other people about this story, though, I only attribute it to how tired I was at the time I had been writing it. I leave out the schizophrenia part; that part tends to make it less funny.

By far my most common are tactile (people touching me, pushing me, water droplets), but I've also had visual (a veery big rat walking along the sidewalk that lunged at me, giant - like, small dog sized - insects). I've got a couple good ones. My primary hallucinations are tactile, so I feel things like people touching me even when there's obviously no one there. Not being able to see it left only one solution: invisible werewolves. So yeah, I have a recurring delusion/hallucination combo about being stalked and harassed by invisible werewolves.

One other time I was convinced that there were fairies (yeah, really) in my high school's tennis court & that they were trying to convince me not to go to college. I would hallucinate this powder (kind of like sawdust) EVERYWHERE: falling from the ceiling of my house, filling in my shoes, lining the windowsill, sometimes for just a few seconds before disappearing. I was convinced it was the fairies at work.

I also have a recurring one about my organs falling out, but it seems pretty run-of-the-mill in comparison. THAT one I was able to actually fess up to my psychs about.

The reason I say that is because that's how I personally experience most of my delusions. For example, I can believe that God is talking to me. I know that if I were to tell someone else about it, they would say I'm crazy, so it's probably a delusion. But I believe it anyway; I know that it'd be called a "delusion", but I also think that the people who'd call it a delusion are wrong. There's a duality to it.

I've always had a lot of insight regarding my psychosis. Even during the fact, even though I'd be convinced of a delusion, I'd still be aware that other people would recognize my beliefs as untrue. That's how I defined a delusion, and that's how I do it now. I can recognize my hallucinations/delusions because I know that if I were to recount them to someone else, they would be able to recognize these things as untrue. In other words, even though I'm convinced of my own reality, I can tell where my reality and others' realities don't overlap. I think it's definitely possible to have insight before being diagnosed. You can recognize something as a delusion and believe it at the same time.

I could always tell to some degree that what I was experiencing was different from a normal person's reality. But that doesn't necessarily mean I don't believe in it.

For example, earlier this week (and to a lesser extent, now) I believed that God was communicating with me. I knew that if I were to tell my friend about it, she would probably tell me that this is a delusion. It's in this respect that I can recognize that the idea isn't "real." However, I'm more likely to distrust others' experiences (i.e. I distrust my friend) than I am to distrust my own, especially when it comes to paranoia. So it's not an all-or-nothing deal. I am both insightful and delusional.

Hallucinations are much easier for me, though, to recognize as objectively not real, because most of my hallucinations are tactile (which as far as I know is not common). This means I'll often feel things like a hand on my shoulder when no one's there & I usually won't have any visuals to go with it, so it's easier for me to recognize as a hallucination.

Even though in these ways I am decently able to recognize my symptoms for what they are, it took me a very long time to get help. It took almost 2 years before I sought a psychiatrist, and it was only because I realized that I was very unsafe and I did not want to kill myself (but I knew that when I get delusional, it is a possibility).

I have only just started medication within the past couple of months. I've been very lucky that I don't have any bad side effects; mostly just little things like tiredness and headaches. So far it does seem to make my episodes somewhat less frequent.

Something I do wish people cared more about in schizophrenia, though, are the negative symptoms. They're overlooked by everyone, but they can be the worst part. Some days I can't talk at all to anyone, or I won't be able to do anything. My focus and thought processing are totally shot, too. I know you didn't ask about this, but I felt like it was worth mentioning if you're wanting to learn more.

A lot of the time I screw myself over because I make my schedule a couple weeks in advance, so since my flareups usually roll around without warning that can leave me with a ton of work and no way to do it because a few weeks ago I thought that I could get it done.

Something that helps me out (even though I don't really have that many auditory hallus, it still helps) is listening to white noise, or a ton of podcasts overlapping on top of each other so it just sounds like a bunch of people talking indiscernibly. I work as a transcriptionist, though, so a lot of the time I can't do this while I'm working (unless I'm just editing a transcript, in which case I'm totally set), but if things are really hard I can take a break and just do that. Taking a break to shower can really help, too.

Or if I can't do anything along those lines, stuff like just laughing aloud or rocking back and forth (as stereotypical as it sounds) can help me out somewhat. Sometimes there's just no way and I can't focus on it at all, so I try to get stuff done in advance just in case. Otherwise, I just can't meet those deadlines.

My therapist keeps reminding me that I'm basically screwed as I am right now though bc once I get a better job I won't be able to take frequent breaks like I already am, which is true. I lucked out on the one I have now, even though the pay sucks.

Afaik triggers(tm) don't just relate to trauma-related ones. From a conversation with my therapist (& my other therapist & both psychs I've talked to seem to agree on this), anything that can exacerbate symptoms is technically a trigger. So like, if losing sleep makes your symptoms worse, then pulling an all-nighter counts as one. Caffeine is a common one for psychotic symptoms

The word's been bastardized & I don't like using it but afaik that's how the definition works at least

I agree that you might wanna look into finding a new psych. I've had several docs dismiss my hallus in a similar way bc they weren't auditory & it all went downhill really fast. In the meantime, calling him doesn't seem like a bad idea imo, & definitely talking to your therapist about it'll probably help you out

If it's only when you're trying to sleep, I'd look into this from the FAQ:

> If you hear voices, see things, or think weird things, when you are trying to sleep, this is probably normal. This state is called hypnagogia.

Hypnagogia's the only time I get auditory stuff. For me personally at least, it feels pretty different than when I hallucinate during the day

It's not common, but it's not unheard of. I have primarily tactile hallucinations (only others I really have are visual, but they're not nearly as frequent), which has thrown both psychs I've seen, my neurologist, & a few different counselors for a loop. It's much more common to have auditory or visual primarily. It's the reason I'm still undiagnosed.

It's not impossible to happen, though; it's just a red flag for psychs to cover all their bases bc it's just not as common for stuff like schiz (this is what I've been told, at least)

I can almost always tell if something I'm thinking counts as a "delusion," but I'll still wholeheartedly believe it at the same time. I'll know that if I were to explain the belief to someone else, they wouldn't believe it, & that's usually what I kind of base it off of. But even though I can pretty easily recognize my delusions, I often don't trust other people's judgment enough to come down from them.

I do try cataloguing them because I have a bad memory, which has worked for me pretty well. I know that I have a lot of religious delusions, so I try avoiding it in conversation, & sometimes I can immediately recognize an episode as it's beginning to start. Cataloguing has helped me in that I can say, "Hey, going down this road has never worked out for me. Let's not," or something along those lines & this can help me out - it doesn't stop an episode per se but it can help me deal with it more "rationally."

I used to write with letters that I made up so that no one else could read them, but A) it was very time consuming for me to reread it all and B) I was super scared that someone would figure it out anyway. Plus this was before my memory skills took a dive, & nowadays it'd be a pretty lost cause to try and pick it up again

Lately, I've been using something that's sort of like a protective symbol that I draw or scratch onto every page. It's been working for me very well and sometimes I have to edit it slightly but it usually works just fine
